milestones.title: Settlement on the Purana Qila mound
milestones.detail: Excavations by the Archaeological Survey of India found continuous habitation on the Purana Qila mound from the Mauryan period onward, through Shunga, Kushana, Gupta, Rajput, Sultanate and Mughal levels.
milestones.source: Press Information Bureau, Government of India (Ministry of Culture), release of 21 June 2023 on the Purana Qila excavation, https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=1934128; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purana_Qila

milestones.title: Lal Kot, the first fortified city of Delhi
milestones.detail: The Tomara king Anangpal built the fort of Lal Kot at Mehrauli in the south of present-day Delhi. It is the first of the successive walled cities of Delhi.
milestones.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Delhi (citing Cohen 1989, Journal of the American Oriental Society)

milestones.title: Delhi Sultanate founded
milestones.detail: After the death of Muhammad of Ghor, Qutb-ud-din Aibak took control of the Indian conquests and made Delhi the capital of a new sultanate.

milestones.title: Tughlaqabad founded
milestones.detail: Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq began the fortified city of Tughlaqabad, in what is now the south of Delhi.

milestones.title: Capital ordered moved to Daulatabad
milestones.detail: Muhammad bin Tughluq ordered the capital moved from Delhi to Daulatabad in the Deccan; Chandler's estimate for Delhi drops sharply for this year.

milestones.title: Timur sacks Delhi
milestones.detail: Timur captured and sacked the city and massacred captives. Chandler puts the population at 125,000 in 1398 and 50,000 in 1450.

milestones.title: Red Fort finished; Shahjahanabad is the capital
milestones.detail: Shah Jahan's Red Fort, begun in 1639, was completed in 1648 as the palace-fort of his new walled city of Shahjahanabad, today's Old Delhi.

milestones.title: Nader Shah sacks Delhi
milestones.detail: After defeating the Mughal army at Karnal, Nader Shah of Persia sacked and looted Delhi and carried off the Peacock Throne.

milestones.title: East India Company takes Delhi
milestones.detail: Company forces defeated the Marathas at the Battle of Delhi during the Second Anglo-Maratha War and took control of the city.

milestones.title: Rebellion and siege of Delhi
milestones.detail: Delhi was a main centre of the Indian Rebellion of 1857; the British retook the city after a siege, and the rebellion's defeat brought direct British rule.

milestones.title: Capital of British India moved to Delhi
milestones.detail: At the Delhi Durbar of December 1911 George V announced the transfer of the capital from Calcutta and laid the foundation stone of New Delhi.

milestones.title: New Delhi inaugurated
milestones.detail: The new capital designed by Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker south of the old city was inaugurated on 13 February 1931.

milestones.title: Partition transforms the city
milestones.detail: During the partition of India about five lakh (500,000) Hindu and Sikh refugees, mainly from West Punjab, arrived in Delhi while about three lakh Muslim residents left for Pakistan.

milestones.title: First Master Plan for Delhi
milestones.detail: The Delhi Development Authority's master plan of 1962 set out the organised development of new land for housing around the city.

milestones.title: Delhi Metro opens
milestones.detail: The Delhi Metro began operation on 24 December 2002.

notes: Scope: Delhi as a whole, not only New Delhi (the UN lists the agglomeration as 'New Delhi'). Start date: the Mahabharata tradition places Indraprastha, the Pandava capital, on the Purana Qila site; that is legend and is not used. The documented start is archaeological: Archaeological Survey of India excavations at Purana Qila (B. B. Lal in 1954-55 and again from 1969, later seasons from 2013) found continuous habitation from the Mauryan period, which the Ministry of Culture summarises as about 2,500 years; an Ashokan rock edict was also found at Srinivaspuri in 1966. The year -300 is a round figure for the Mauryan levels, not a dated event, so the start is marked estimated. Painted Grey Ware sherds (roughly 1000 BCE) have been found on the mound but not yet in a secure stratified context, so they are not used. If a firm founding of a named city is preferred, the alternative is 1052 CE, when the Tomara king Anangpal built Lal Kot. Historic core: the successive cities of Delhi stood in different places (Lal Kot at Mehrauli and Tughlaqabad in the south, Purana Qila and Firoz Shah Kotla further north near the Yamuna). The core given is the Red Fort in Shahjahanabad, the walled city of 1648 from which the modern city grew continuously; earlier population points refer to the capital of their day, up to 15 km to the south. Population: there is no estimate between the start and 1052. Points from 1052 to 1853 are Chandler's estimates as digitised by Reba et al. Two values in the digitised file were left out as probably erroneous or unverifiable against the printed book: 1,250,000 for 1375 (the neighbouring years give 125,000) and 8,000 for 1596. The 1846 and 1853 figures look like enumerations but were only seen through Chandler. The 1881 and 1891 censuses are for Delhi city as printed in the Imperial Gazetteer of 1908; no figure for the 1868 Punjab census or the 1872 census was found. The 1901-1941 points are the Census of India's own back-series for the Delhi urban agglomeration (Table A-4, 2011), which fits the UN series from 1950. Landmarks: heights for the Red Fort, Purana Qila and Tughlaqabad are wall heights; the Rashtrapati Bhavan height has no primary citation. Left out for lack of a sourced height or position: Safdarjung's Tomb, Jantar Mantar, the Parliament buildings, and the Civic Centre (112 m, 2010; listed by the CTBUH Skyscraper Center without coordinates). The CTBUH database lists almost nothing else for Delhi proper; the tall towers of the region are in Noida and Gurgaon, outside the city.
